event: Nala wakes at dusk on cold wet shingle, barefoot, in a thin soaked linen shift and nothing else.
Her last memory is Alan dozing over a book at his back window one evening.
A white stone tower with a red iron cap stands on the rock above the cove.
She sits up; long dark red hair slaps wet against her back and sticks to her face.
Her hands are small, pale and freckled; when she swears aloud, the voice is a woman's.
Under the wet shift she feels small soft breasts, and a pussy where Alan's cock was.
She thinks of herself as Nala, and the name feels like her own.
The cold takes hold; she shakes hard and can no longer feel her feet.
Up on the tower the lamp catches, and the great lens begins to turn.
The beam sweeps over a reef of black rocks offshore, then across the cove and over her.
A lantern starts down the steep steps cut into the rock.
A tall woman reaches her: navy jumper, sea boots, a thick dark braid over one shoulder.
The woman holds the lantern to Nala's face and asks sharply whether she came off a boat.
Nala says she doesn't know, starts to say she was somewhere else, stops, and gives only "Nala".
The woman says she is Morwenna, keeper of the light, and no boat went on the Teeth today.
Morwenna pulls off her jumper and drags it over Nala's head without asking.
It is warm from Morwenna's body, smells of wool and lamp oil, and hangs to Nala's knees.
Nala tries to stand, and her numb feet fold under her.
Morwenna hooks Nala's arm over her shoulders and half carries her up the rock steps.
Nala's head reaches only Morwenna's chin; she has never been this small beside anyone.
Morwenna's hand on her waist is cold through the wool, and steady.
The keeper's cottage at the tower's foot: granite walls, slate roof, one hearth, one bed.
Two goats bleat from a shed; Morwenna hushes them by name, gentler than she spoke to Nala.
Morwenna builds the fire high and sets a kettle and a pot of fish stew over it.
She hands Nala a dry shift and a blanket, and turns her back while Nala changes.
Nala peels off the wet shift by the fire and sees this body whole for the first time.
Pale freckled skin pebbled with cold, pink nipples tight, a tuft of dark red hair over her pussy.
She stares too long; Morwenna, back still turned, asks dryly whether she is decent yet.
Nala scrambles into the shift and blanket and says yes.
Morwenna sits her in the one chair by the fire and puts a mug of hot tea in her hands.
Morwenna kneels and chafes Nala's bare feet between her own cold, calloused hands.
Feeling comes back as pain; Nala hisses, and Morwenna does not let go.
Nala watches the thin pale scar through the end of Morwenna's left eyebrow while she works.
Morwenna glances up and catches her looking; Nala looks away first, her face hot.
Over stew Morwenna asks where she is from; Nala says far away, and she doesn't know how she came.
Morwenna says flatly that the tide leaves in that cove whatever the sea gives up.
She adds that old women in town say the Morrow Head lamp calls home what the sea has lost.
Nala asks if she believes it; Morwenna says she believes in oil and clockwork.
Nala asks where she is; Morwenna names Penmorrow, a mile south along the cliff path.
Nala thanks her warmly, then again; Morwenna tells her not to make a fuss of it.
Morwenna says she will walk her to Penmorrow in the morning; someone there may know something.
Warm at last, Nala laughs at how high her own laugh sounds; Morwenna's mouth twitches.
Morwenna says she must go up and wind the lamp's clockwork, as she does every four hours.
Nala offers to come; Morwenna says not up ninety-six steps on those feet.
Alone by the fire, Nala hears Morwenna's voice faint down the stairwell, talking to the lamp.
She catches Morwenna telling the lamp there is a girl in her chair and she doesn't know why.
Morwenna comes down and makes up the straw mattress in the loft with spare blankets.
Nala climbs to the loft, and Morwenna hands up her own pillow after her.
Their fingers meet on the pillow; Morwenna's are cold, and neither lets go at once.
Morwenna says "Goodnight, Nala", the first time she has said the name.
In the loft Nala lies listening to the sea, the lamp's glow moving on the slates above her.
She lays a hand on her own chest, feels her heart small and quick, and thinks of Morwenna's hands.
She falls asleep not knowing whether she will wake as Nala or as Alan.
